title: Organizing Digital Files
subtitle: A file you cannot find is a file you do not have.
objectives: Build a folder structure from widest to narrowest
Name a file so it says what it is
Explain why dates go at the front of a filename
Explain the difference between deleting and archiving
Explain why one copy is not a backup

cards.title: Untitled document (3)
cards.text: Everyone has these. The file is not lost, and you still cannot find it, which comes to the same thing.

cards.title: Messy, sorted, named, backed up
cards.text: Tap through all four. The naming screen is the one worth copying exactly.

cards.title: A good name answers three questions
cards.text: When was it, what subject is it, and what is it. In that order, every time.

question.explain: Date, subject, then what it is. It tells you everything without opening it.

cards.title: Because the computer sorts alphabetically
cards.text: Written as year, then month, then day, an alphabetical sort is also a date sort. That is the whole trick.
points: **Every file lands in order** with no effort.
**This is why the format looks backwards.**

cards.title: Your saves already do this
cards.text: Every game names its saves with a slot and a timestamp, because a list of files called 'save' is useless.
points: **The camera writes the date into the name.**

question.text: Writing a date as year-month-day makes an alphabetical sort work as a date sort.
question.explain: That is exactly why the format looks backwards. 2026-09-04 sorts before 2026-09-11.

cards.title: Halfway
cards.text: Part 2 is folders, archiving and backups. Look away from the screen for a bit.

cards.title: Widest first, narrowest last
cards.text: School, then the year, then the subject. Three levels is almost always enough.

cards.title: Too many levels is its own problem
cards.text: Every extra level is another decision when you save, and another guess when you look.
points: **A folder with one file** should not exist.

cards.title: Archive is not the same as delete
cards.text: Archiving moves something out of the way and keeps it. Deleting means it is gone.

question.text: What should you do with last term's finished work?
options: Archive it into a folder for that term
question.explain: Archiving moves it out of the way but keeps it. When unsure, archive rather than delete.

cards.title: The worst version of this is losing a draft
cards.text: Writers lose work to a dead laptop, not to bad writing. One copy in one place is one accident from nothing.
points: **Cloud storage counts** as a second place.
**A folder on the same computer does not.**

cards.title: One copy is not a copy
cards.text: A backup only counts if it survives whatever kills the original. Same machine means same accident.
points: **Laptop plus cloud** is the easy version.
**Add a USB drive** for anything important.
**Check it opens.** An unreadable backup is none.

cards.title: The Space Shuttle flew with five computers
cards.text: Four ran the same program and voted. A fifth ran different software, in case a bug broke the other four.
points: **Four identical machines** agreeing was the check.
**A backup must fail differently** to count.

question.text: Why is a second folder on the same laptop not a backup?
options: The same accident destroys both copies
question.explain: A backup has to survive whatever kills the original. Same machine, same accident.

terms.def: An agreed pattern for names: date, subject, what it is.
Folders inside folders, arranged widest first.
Move something out of the way but keep it.
A second copy stored somewhere the first accident cannot reach.
Files kept on a service's computers, reachable from anywhere.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Date, subject, what it is.** No spaces.
**Two places**, one of them not the laptop.

quiz.text: What order should a filename use?
options: Date, then subject, then what it is
What it is, then the date
quiz.explain: It answers when, what subject and what it is, without you opening the file.
quiz.objective: Name a file so it says what it is

quiz.text: Why is 2026-09-04 better than 04-09-2026 in a filename?
options: An alphabetical sort then puts the files in date order
Computers cannot read the other format
quiz.explain: Year first, then month, then day. That is why the format looks backwards.
quiz.objective: Explain why dates go at the front of a filename

quiz.text: What should you use instead of spaces in a filename?
quiz.explain: Hyphens keep the name readable and avoid problems in links and older systems.
quiz.objective: Name a file so it says what it is

quiz.text: How should a folder structure be arranged?
quiz.explain: School, then year, then subject. Three levels is almost always enough.
quiz.objective: Build a folder structure from widest to narrowest

quiz.text: More folder levels always makes files easier to find.
quiz.explain: False. Every extra level is another decision when saving and another guess when looking.
quiz.objective: Build a folder structure from widest to narrowest

quiz.text: A folder containing a single file usually means what?
quiz.explain: A folder with one file adds a level for nothing. A folder with ninety needs splitting.
quiz.objective: Build a folder structure from widest to narrowest

quiz.text: What is the difference between archiving and deleting?
options: Archiving keeps the file but moves it out of the way
quiz.explain: When you are unsure which one to do, archive.
quiz.objective: Explain the difference between deleting and archiving

quiz.text: What should you do with last term's completed work?
options: Print it and delete the file
quiz.explain: It is finished but not worthless. Archiving keeps it without cluttering this term.
quiz.objective: Explain the difference between deleting and archiving

quiz.text: A copy in a second folder on the same laptop counts as a backup.
quiz.explain: False. A backup has to survive whatever kills the original. Same machine means same accident.
quiz.objective: Explain why one copy is not a backup

quiz.text: What is the simplest workable backup setup?
quiz.explain: Two places at least, and one of them not the laptop. A USB drive can be a third.
quiz.objective: Explain why one copy is not a backup

quiz.text: Why should you open a backup occasionally?
options: An unreadable backup is not a backup
It keeps the file from expiring
quiz.explain: Checking it opens is part of having one. Do it before you need it.
quiz.objective: Explain why one copy is not a backup

quiz.text: Why does a badly named file cause a problem later?
options: You have to open several files to find the right one
quiz.explain: The file is not lost, and you still cannot find it. That comes to the same thing.
quiz.objective: Name a file so it says what it is

teacher.summary: Week 8 covers digital file organisation, and it is one of the few genuinely transferable skills in the whole TLE strand — the naming convention taught here is the one used professionally. The ISO-style date is explained by its mechanism rather than asserted, which is what makes it stick: alphabetical sorting becomes date sorting for free. The archive-versus-delete distinction and the definition of a backup as 'a copy that survives what kills the original' are both worth him keeping well past Grade 6.
discussion: Ask him to open his Downloads folder and read out three filenames. The lesson usually makes itself.
Ask why the date format looks backwards and what it buys.
Ask what would be lost right now if his laptop stopped working today.
Ask him to name where his second copy of anything actually lives.
teacher.extension: Have him build the three-level folder structure for this term and rename ten real files into the convention. Ten is enough to make the pattern automatic.
misconceptions: 'The file is not lost, so it is fine.' A file you cannot find is a file you do not have.
'Deeper folders are more organised.' Every level adds a decision and a guess.
'A second copy on the same computer is a backup.' One accident takes both.
'Archiving and deleting are the same.' Archiving keeps the file; deleting ends it.
